_comment: The full approvals path for an Alberta data centre, provincial through municipal, ending at occupancy. A MAP OF PROCESS, not legal advice: it shows who decides what, what must precede what, and what can run in parallel. Every node links to the body that runs it so a reader can start there. Durations are deliberately absent — they vary by project and queue position, and quoting one would be inventing a number.
title: From first enquiry to occupancy
intro: A data centre needs approvals from four different authorities on four different clocks. Most can run in parallel — and must, because the grid connection is almost always the long pole. This shows the whole path, what blocks what, and where each process is actually started.
caution: A map of the process, not legal advice. Confirm each requirement against the authority named before relying on it.

lanes.label: Grid connection
lanes.note: Almost always the longest path. Start it first.
lanes.levelNote: Provincial system operator and a regulated utility. The municipality is a stakeholder here, not the decision-maker.

offgrid.label: On-site power
offgrid.body: Proponent, fuel supplier and the AER
offgrid.note: No queue to wait in — and no queue to pace the project either.
offgrid.levelNote: Provincial regulators, but not the system operator: the AESO has no role where there is no connection.

lanes.label: Utilities regulator
lanes.note: Approves the substation, any on-site generation, and the industrial system question — never the building.
lanes.levelNote: Provincial quasi-judicial regulator. Its decisions are made under provincial statute, not the land use bylaw.

lanes.label: Land, water & consultation
lanes.body: Alberta Environment and Protected Areas, and other provincial authorities
lanes.note: Runs on its own clock. Two of these gate ground disturbance; the rest gate provincial decisions or operation, not your permit.
lanes.levelNote: Provincial department. Independent of the municipal land use decision.

lanes.label: Municipal
lanes.note: Land use, servicing, and the conditions you can actually enforce.
lanes.levelNote: Your authority. Council and the development authority, under the Municipal Government Act.

lanes.label: Building & safety
lanes.note: Follows the development permit and ends at occupancy.
lanes.levelNote: Provincial statute, usually administered municipally: the Safety Codes Act is provincial, but most municipalities are accredited to issue and inspect. Confirm who is accredited in your jurisdiction — it is not the same everywhere.

phases.label: Phase 6
phases.name: Lifecycle & decommissioning
phases.sub: After the building is in use

nodes.title: System access service request
nodes.what: Ask AESO for transmission system access. This opens the queue position that everything downstream depends on.
nodes.why: The single longest lead item on the project, and the one most often started too late. A queue position obtained in month one is worth more than any amount of expediting later.

nodes.title: System study & connection proposal
nodes.what: AESO and the transmission facility owner determine the point of interconnection, the substation required, and any system reinforcement.
nodes.why: This output defines the substation footprint, which the municipal site plan has to accommodate. Getting it before the development permit is drawn saves a redesign.

nodes.title: Connection agreement & cost commitment
nodes.what: The proponent accepts the connection proposal, enters the system access service agreement with AESO, and posts the security and construction contribution that lets the transmission facility owner begin work.
nodes.why: This is where a grid connection stops being an enquiry and becomes a commitment. Until it is signed and secured, a queue position is not a connection — an application that presents an AESO study as though it were an approval is overstating what it holds. Ask what has actually been executed. In the same phase, and separately, the AUC decides the substation itself.
nodes.watch: Confirm the current instrument name and the security terms against the AESO tariff before relying on them — the sequence is stable, the naming has changed before.

nodes.title: Substation construction
nodes.what: The transmission facility owner builds the substation and connection under the Commission's approval, and against whatever commitment AESO requires before work starts, on the grid's schedule.
nodes.why: Two things gate this, not one: the AUC permit for the facility, and the proponent's commitment to AESO. Either one outstanding stops the build, which is why two arrows converge here. Confirm the form the commitment takes — see the previous step.

nodes.title: Energization
nodes.what: Power is available at the site.
nodes.why: A finished building with no firm connection is a stranded asset. Tying occupancy — not construction — to evidence of energization is enforceable and within municipal jurisdiction.

nodes.title: Islanded supply concept
nodes.what: Settle how the site will be powered with no transmission connection: plant size and redundancy, the fuel supply and how firm it is, and whether a connection to the AESO system is intended in any later phase.
nodes.why: The entire difference between the two routes is decided here, and it is decided by the applicant rather than by you. Get it in writing at pre-application: "off-grid" in a submission sometimes means "off-grid for phase one", and a project that intends to connect later is a grid project on a delay and should be assessed as one.
nodes.watch: Any standby, backup or import arrangement is a connection. A site that can draw from the system at all, however rarely, is not islanded and the AESO steps come back.
nodes.startLabel: Alberta — build your AI data centre

nodes.title: Fuel supply & pipeline
nodes.what: Where the plant burns natural gas, the line that feeds it is a pipeline licensed by the AER, and both the licence and firm supply have to be in place before the plant can run.
nodes.why: This is the off-grid project’s long pole — the item that replaces the transmission connection and cannot be shortened by wanting it sooner. Ask whether the pipeline licence and a firm supply contract exist, not whether gas is "available in the area".
nodes.watch: Which approvals a particular line needs depends on its size, pressure and route. Confirm the requirement with the AER rather than from this diagram.

nodes.title: Plant & substation construction
nodes.what: The generating units, the on-site substation and the wires between them are built under the Commission’s approvals.
nodes.why: Three separate things gate this and none of them is the grid: the power plant approval, the substation permit, and a fuel supply that is actually contracted.

nodes.title: Plant commissioning
nodes.what: The plant is commissioned and the site has power.
nodes.why: The occupancy test is the same as on the grid route — evidence that firm power exists — but the evidence is different. Here it is a commissioned plant and a contracted fuel supply, not an energized connection.

nodes.title: Participant involvement programme
nodes.what: Notification and consultation with landowners and occupants within the rule's radius, before the facility application is filed.
nodes.why: Ask to be included. The AUC's notification radius and the municipality's differ, and residents notified by one process and not the other is the most common source of 'nobody told us' at a public hearing.
nodes.watch: Rule 007 governs this. Its own page could not be reached at a stable URL when this was last checked, so the link goes to the AUC's rules index — open Rule 007 from there and read the current edition.

nodes.title: Facility application
nodes.what: Application for the substation, with the noise assessment required by the Commission's noise rule. A power plant on the same site is a separate application — see the generation chain below.
nodes.why: The noise study filed here is usually the only acoustic modelling in existence before the municipality has to decide. Read it.

nodes.title: Permit & licence
nodes.what: The Commission decides, and attaches its own conditions on siting, noise and reclamation.
nodes.why: Compare these conditions with your draft conditions. Where the AUC has imposed a stricter limit, adopt it by reference rather than writing a weaker parallel one.

nodes.title: Indigenous consultation
nodes.what: Consultation on provincial decisions that may affect treaty rights and traditional uses, run by the Crown with parts of the procedural work usually carried by the proponent.
nodes.why: It is absent from most application packages and it is the item most likely to move a provincial decision date the municipal file depends on. Ask at pre-application whether consultation has been triggered, who is running it, and what stage it has reached — you are not the decision-maker, but you are entitled to know whether the provincial approvals your permit assumes are exposed.
nodes.watch: Whether consultation is triggered, and by which decision, is determined by the Crown and is fact-specific. Do not conclude from this card that a given project does or does not require it — ask Indigenous Relations and your solicitor.

nodes.title: Roadside development permit
nodes.what: A provincial permit for development within the controlled area of a provincial highway, including access, signage and setbacks.
nodes.why: A common referral and a common surprise. Where it applies, the access arrangement the province will accept can differ from the one drawn on the site plan, and a data centre's construction and generator-fuel traffic makes access a live issue rather than a formality.
nodes.watch: Whether a site is inside the controlled area depends on its distance from the highway and from an intersection. Confirm with Transportation and Economic Corridors rather than from this card.

nodes.title: Public land disposition
nodes.what: A disposition where any part of the project — the site, an access road, a pipeline or a transmission line — crosses Crown land.
nodes.why: Easy to miss because it usually attaches to the linear works rather than the site. A permitted building served by an unauthorised crossing is not deliverable, and the disposition has to precede any disturbance on Crown land.
nodes.watch: Applies only where Crown land is actually engaged. Confirm the land status before assuming either way.

nodes.title: Water Act licence or approval
nodes.what: Required where the project draws groundwater or surface water rather than a municipal supply.
nodes.why: A permit granted against an unlicensed supply is not deliverable. Ask whether a licence or transfer is in hand and whether its volume matches the stated use.

nodes.title: Environmental & historical clearances
nodes.what: Wetland assessment, environmental approvals where thresholds are engaged, and Historical Resources Act clearance.
nodes.why: These run on their own timetable, independent of the land use decision — but clearance has to be in hand before the ground is disturbed, which is why the arrow runs to site grading rather than to the permit. They rarely stop a project and they routinely delay one.
nodes.watch: Historical Resources Act clearance is part of this, but no stable page for it resolved when this was last checked. Ask Environment and Protected Areas which clearances a given site engages.

nodes.title: Pre-application meeting
nodes.what: Confirm the land use district, whether the use is permitted or discretionary, servicing capacity, and whether a statutory plan amendment is needed.
nodes.why: Municipal leverage is at its highest here and falls steadily afterwards. Establish the ultimate build-out load, not the first phase, and get it in writing.

nodes.title: Redesignation or plan amendment
nodes.what: Land use bylaw amendment, and any area structure plan amendment, where the current designation does not accommodate the use.
nodes.why: Only some projects need this. Where it is needed it adds a council process and a public hearing, and it is the point at which the community has a statutory voice.

nodes.title: Development permit application
nodes.what: The formal application, circulation and referrals.
nodes.why: Decide here whether the substation forms part of this application or a separate provincial one, and say so in writing. The substation is approved by the AUC; this permit is not that approval.

nodes.title: Decision & development agreement
nodes.what: The permit decision with conditions, and the agreement fixing servicing, off-site levies, road use and security.
nodes.why: The agreement outlasts the permit and is the most durable instrument the municipality holds. Cost recovery is secured here or not at all.

nodes.title: 21-day SDAB appeal window
nodes.what: The decision does not take effect while the appeal period runs, and an appeal to the board suspends it further until the board has decided.
nodes.why: A hard date on the timeline that no party can compress. Applicants routinely programme construction from the decision date rather than from the end of the appeal period, and that is where the schedule in an application first goes wrong. Note also that a permit for a permitted use that complies with the bylaw is appealable only on narrow grounds — the waiting period still runs either way.
nodes.watch: The period runs under the Municipal Government Act, but when it starts, who may appeal, and what the permit can and cannot support in the meantime are specifics to confirm against the Act and your own bylaw. Do not take the number off this card.

nodes.title: Post financial security
nodes.what: Where the development agreement requires it, an irrevocable letter of credit or other security covering servicing, offsite improvements, road use and reclamation, posted before site work begins.
nodes.why: The agreement is where cost recovery is secured or lost, and the security is the part that actually bites. Size it against real servicing and reclamation cost rather than a nominal figure, and check the instrument is irrevocable and cannot expire before the obligation it covers.
nodes.watch: Whether security is required, in what form and in what amount is set by your own agreement and policy, not by this diagram.

nodes.title: Site grading
nodes.what: Stripping and earthworks, often begun before the building permit issues.
nodes.why: Once a large site is stripped, refusing what follows becomes far harder to defend. Require security sized to actual reclamation cost and a drainage design that works as a standalone end state.

nodes.title: Building & trade permits
nodes.what: Building permit, then electrical, plumbing and gas permits under the Safety Codes Act.

nodes.title: Inspections
nodes.what: Staged inspections through construction.

nodes.title: Occupancy permit
nodes.what: Legal occupation of the building.
nodes.why: More than one authority has to be satisfied before this issues: the Safety Codes inspections, the power supply, and — through the building permit — the municipal decision. The power supply is the one most likely to be outstanding.

nodes.title: Power plant application
nodes.what: A separate application under the Hydro and Electric Energy Act where the project proposes on-site generation, including gas-fired plant serving the load. Small units may be exempt — confirm the current threshold rather than assuming every unit needs an application.
nodes.why: This is a different application from the substation, with its own record, its own noise and emissions case, and often its own hearing. A project can win one and lose the other — as the Olds decision showed.

nodes.title: Power plant approval & licence
nodes.what: The Commission's decision on the generating facility, with its own conditions on siting, noise, emissions and reclamation.
nodes.why: Approval here authorises the generating facility. It does not authorise the buildings, access, or site development around it — those remain municipal, which is why the paired municipal permit exists.

nodes.title: Industrial system designation
nodes.what: An application for the Commission to designate the site as an industrial system, so that the plant, the substation and the wires between them are treated as one industrial operation rather than as a utility serving customers.
nodes.why: This decides whether the electrical infrastructure on the site is yours to condition as land use or the Commission’s to regulate as a utility. Ask at pre-application which route the applicant is taking, because the answer changes who sets the conditions on the substation.
nodes.watch: Whether a designation is required is fact-specific. AUC Rule 007 covers industrial system designations alongside power plants and substations, but confirm the current requirement with the Commission and your solicitor rather than from this diagram.

nodes.title: Designation order
nodes.what: The Commission’s decision on the designation, and any conditions attached to it.
nodes.why: Read it alongside the power plant approval. Between them they fix what the Commission has taken responsibility for, and everything they do not cover is still yours.

nodes.title: Development permit — generation facility
nodes.what: Where the land use bylaw requires it, the municipal permit for the generating facility and its site works — a separate file from the data centre's own development permit.
nodes.why: An AUC approval for a power plant does not remove the municipal approvals that go with building it — the site development, access and associated works still come to you. Treat it as its own file with its own conditions, not as a footnote to the data centre permit.
nodes.watch: How a provincial approval interacts with municipal land use authority is addressed in the Municipal Government Act, and the effect is fact-specific. Confirm the current position with your solicitor before concluding what you can and cannot condition.

nodes.title: End-of-life facility management
nodes.what: The obligations that run once the building is in use: monitoring and reporting commitments, equipment replacement cycles, and the trigger points that start decommissioning.
nodes.why: Data centre equipment turns over far faster than the building around it. A permit that ends at occupancy leaves the municipality with no instrument for what happens across the next twenty years, which is why the obligations have to be written into the agreement while there is still leverage.
nodes.watch: Nothing here is a standing legal requirement. What applies to a given site is whatever the development agreement, and the Commission's conditions, actually say.

nodes.title: Reclamation execution
nodes.what: Decommissioning and site reclamation to the standard set in the development agreement and, for the generating and transmission facilities, in the Commission's own reclamation conditions.
nodes.why: The standard reached here was fixed years earlier, in the development agreement and in the security posted against it. That is the whole argument for negotiating decommissioning at the agreement stage rather than leaving it to a future council.
nodes.watch: Reclamation for the power plant and the substation sits with the Commission, not with you. Read its conditions alongside your agreement so the two do not contradict.

insights.title: The grid is the critical path
insights.text: Every other approval can usually be obtained faster than a transmission connection. If the AESO request has not been made, the project timeline in the application is unsupported — regardless of how advanced the design is.

insights.title: The grid track does not stop at the study
insights.text: The system study is the middle of the grid path, not the end of it. What follows is the connection agreement and cost commitment, the AUC’s decision on the substation, construction by the transmission facility owner, and finally energization — which is what occupancy should be conditioned on.

insights.title: Four things should start in week one
insights.text: The AESO request, the municipal pre-application, any water licence, and the AUC participant involvement programme are all independent of each other. Running them in sequence rather than in parallel adds months for no reason.

insights.title: How to read a pair letter
insights.text: Two cards carrying the same letter are two separate applications, to two different authorities, for the same physical thing on one site — one pair is the substation, the other the on-site power plant. Both are required, and neither authorises the other: a decision on one does not oblige the other to follow. There is no order between them, which is why they carry a letter rather than an arrow — they can be filed and decided in either sequence, or at the same time. It matters because holding the provincial permit is not holding the municipal one, and a project can win one and lose the other. Check that the site plan filed with each shows the same footprint and that the conditions do not contradict, and reconcile them at pre-application rather than at decision.

insights.title: A power plant needs both approvals
insights.text: Where a project proposes on-site generation, the AUC approves the generating facility and the municipality still permits the site development around it. They are separate files on separate records, marked here by a shared pair letter on both cards. Neither one authorises the other.

insights.title: Two approvals, one site
insights.text: The municipality approves the building; the AUC approves the substation that powers it. Neither authorises the other, and both site plans must show the same footprint — reconcile them at pre-application, not at decision.

insights.title: Occupancy is the real gate
insights.text: Construction can finish while the power is still outstanding — an unfinished connection on the grid route, an uncommissioned plant or an unsecured fuel supply off it. Conditioning occupancy, rather than construction, on evidence of firm power is enforceable, within municipal jurisdiction, and prevents a stranded building.

insights.title: Off the grid is not off the hook
insights.text: Taking the AESO out of the picture removes one lane and nothing else. The power plant approval stops being conditional and becomes the project’s licence to operate at all, the industrial system question appears, and every municipal and building approval is exactly as it was. What changes is the timing, not the scope.

insights.title: The queue was doing you a favour
insights.text: On the grid route the connection queue paces the project, and a permit decision has years of construction runway behind it. Off-grid there is no queue. The municipal decision can become the earliest binding date on the file, so conditions and the development agreement carry weight they would not otherwise have to.

insights.title: Test the claim that a site is islanded
insights.text: Ask three things in writing: is there any standby, backup or import arrangement; is a connection intended in a later phase; and what serves the load when the plant is down. Any of the three can turn an off-grid project back into a grid one. Note also that the province’s computing equipment levy is tiered by whether a facility is grid-connected, which gives an applicant a reason to describe a project as off-grid — the levy detail on the rules page is media-reported rather than primary, so read it at source before relying on it.

insights.title: A different week-one list
insights.text: Off-grid the four independent starts change: the municipal pre-application, the AUC participant involvement programme for the power plant, the islanded supply concept and the fuel enquiry behind it, and any water licence. The AESO request is not among them — and its absence is exactly why this route can arrive faster than a municipality expects.

levels.label: Provincial
levels.note: Decided under provincial statute. You are consulted, not deciding.

levels.label: Municipal
levels.note: Decided by council or the development authority under the MGA.

levels.label: Provincial statute, municipal administration
levels.note: Provincial rules, usually applied by an accredited municipality.

variants.label: Grid-connected
variants.intro: A data centre needs approvals from four different authorities on four different clocks. Most can run in parallel — and must, because the grid connection is almost always the long pole. This shows the whole path, what blocks what, and where each process is actually started.
variants.note: Load served from the AESO transmission system through a substation built by the transmission facility owner.

variants.label: Off-grid — on-site generation only
variants.intro: The same site with no connection to the AESO system: generation on site feeds the substation, and the substation feeds the load. The whole grid lane falls away and the AESO steps with it. Nothing municipal falls away — and because the connection queue is no longer setting the pace, the municipal decision can become the earliest binding date on the file.
variants.note: Load served entirely by generation on the site. No system access service, no transmission connection, no queue.
